Some of my most used Excel functions, as someone who has spent over 10,000 hours in Excel:

* =XLOOKUP / =INDEX(MATCH()) - Used to look up a specific value and return the corresponding item

* =SUMIFS(Sum Range, Criteria 1 Range, Criteria 1…) - Used to sum a range based on specific criteria

* =COUNTIFS - Same concept as =SUMIFS, but used to count instead of sum

* =XIRR(Values, Dates) - Takes a range of cash flows and corresponding dates to calculate internal rate of return

* =RRI (Number of Periods, Present Value, Future Value) - Used to calculate compound annual growth rate or “CAGR”

* =IF(Logic, True Value, False Value) - Checks for a certain logical condition then returns a value if true or false

* =IFERROR(Value, Value If Error) - Used to make sure an error is not returned, returns a specific value instead of an error

Where I Went To Teach Myself About Finance

1. Investopedia: As the name implies, this is like wikipedia but with a finance focus. It’s great for understanding general concepts, so if you’re ever stuck on a concept that you’re studying either for interviews, coursework, etc. this is a great resource to learn concepts in an easy to understand way. It’s not going to have crazy depth, but this should help you simplify things if you’re stuck.

2. Mergers & Inquisitions: Great resource to prepare in a weekend for a finance interview. Good combination of behavioral and technical questions to study. More of a memorization exercise than actually helping learn concepts. 

3. Peak Frameworks: This is mostly focused around technicals and modeling - the guy who teaches a lot of it is an absolute unit. It will be hugely beneficial to understand technically what’s going on once you’re on the job or if you are doing case studies as part of PE recruiting

4. WSO: Wall Street Oasis (“WSO”) is an online forum for discussing finance (private equity, etc). It’s a nice resource to learn about qualitative things within the industry (culture, work/life balance, etc) but take everything you read with a grain of salt. It’s anonymous and the internet so it can be hit or miss with some really helpful and insightful information, but can also be useless garbage (so be careful!)

I get asked all the time if I would work in Investment Banking if I had to start all over again… so here’s my honest answer:

I was the perfect combination of everything that makes people go down this path: 1) surrounded by money, but didn’t have it myself, 2) a chip on my shoulder & a desire to prove to myself I could do something challenging, and 3) most importantly a naivety of what was ahead of me.

I wanted something meritocratic that had the potential to pay well if I worked hard. And that’s how banking is described to many college kids - the land of meritocracy. This couldn’t be farther from the truth, as I would soon learn, but over time I’ve come to appreciate that even with the nepotism, office politics, and blatant favoritism - it is still one of the most meritocratic industries to start your career in.

I knew, like I think most people do going in, that it was going to be hard. But there is no easy way to replicate what a 100+ hour work week feels like in college. Nothing had really come close to challenging me the way banking did, and then on top of it all COVID happened within my first full year.

I packed up my bags and moved back in with my parents… one more tally for the Jonathan pity points as my adult life was in shambles. Ironically, the fact that COVID happened made my perceived social and personal opportunity cost go down - “every 20 something year old isn’t having fun, but at least i’m not having fun while progressing my career!!”.

And I’m glad I stuck it out - banking paid me well, set me up on a career trajectory that paid me even better, and made me mature into a man… so for that I’m grateful. But, knowing what I know on the other end of it all - I’m not sure that I would voluntarily subject myself to something like that again.

But that’s the irony - I only did it because I didn’t know, and I only know because I did it.

Long story, short - best decision I’ll never make again.

It’s like college but with adult money

The golf classes cost extra relative to normal classes, luckily I was was on financial aid so I got to go to them for free.

I did it because I was going back full time to an investment bank, and thought being able to play golf would help me network or get invited to important work events.

Turns out, junior people are essentially never invited to any golf event - you would need to be an actual scratch golfer to get invited… and even then it’s just to show you off.

Even at the senior level, the idea that people are playing golf 3-4 days a week is far fetched, and the majority of people didn’t play… even casually.

MBA associates are often viewed as liabilities on the job at first, even relative to 2nd year analysts - there is a lot of friction between Analysts, A to A Associates, and MBA associates because MBA associates haven’t “proven themselves yet” or demonstrated they can successfully operate in that environment

Search firms gate keep most buy-side jobs like private equity and hedge funds, there aren’t job postings or open application portals. You often have to be vetted by one of these search firms to even have the opportunity to apply to these roles

Nepotism is real, even if it isn’t directly a family member - most people who get these jobs are very well connected… meaning the pool of openings for non nepo hires is even smaller

Time stamping culture is incredibly prevalent, which basically means juniors will almost always try to send an email right before the log off for the night to senior people to “timestamp” that they were working late

No facial hair, hair that covers your ears, or flashy clothing or watches (french cuffs, Rolex’s, and designer loafers / ties) while you are junior - it’s either viewed as unprofessional or infringing upon the attire of senior folks

Junior bankers always carry the bags… what does that mean - it means before going to client meetings and after staying up all night, junior bankers will be responsible for going to the print room to print all the decks - then physically carry them to the meeting in their bag to hand out to everyone

How To Make Working on Wall Street (Or Any Demanding Job) Sustainable

1. Put the phone down, PUT IT DOWN, if you have a birthday or a wedding or a graduation - put the phone on silent and do not check it - you have to prioritize important life events
2. Protect what is important you – for me it’s video games and the gym. Find the simple hobbies that you can do almost every day and protect them. Find time to work out or hop on a game with friends every once in a while
3. Learn to say no… there’s a saying that the reward for good work is, you guessed it, MORE WORK – when you are at capacity, learn to say no to things
4. Try to eat healthy and exercise, you would be surprised how much even going for a walk or a light run helps when you’ve been sitting at a desk for 16 hours a day
5. Realize tough times are just a moment in time – all things eventually come to pass, just try to take a step back, take a deep breath, and realize you’ll get through this

Things that were normalized on Wall Street

* No one takes a vacation… almost ever. Your first year, managers will deny almost every request you make to take even a week off and generally after your first year, you get 1 full week (5 business days) off during the summer, and a handful of long weekends. There’s also an order to it - where multiple people can’t take the same week off and more senior people pick their vacations first… so you basically get whatever is left over
* Getting out before midnight is considered “early”. I knew it was going to be a rough ride when talking to one of the VPs I said I had been leaving at 2-3am every night that week… and their response was ok i’ll try to aim to let you get out by midnight a few nights… WHAT
* Forget the freshman 15, I gained 20+ pounds my first year on the job mostly as a function of rarely exercising, not sleeping, not getting my steps in, and eating almost every meal at my desk.. fun!
* The vest memes are accurate, almost everyone at least owns a vest and most wear one at least on a weekly basis. One of my good friends used to refer to his vest as his suit of armor 😂

1. I realized there is only one person that can be (and needs to be) there for you at all times… and that’s yourself. That’s not to say you can’t rely on friends and family - but there will only be one person on this earth that is with you every minute of every hour of every day from the first to the last, and that’s yourself. I used to rely on the counsel of others for all my important decisions, even if I didn’t agree with them, but now I’m not afraid to go down the path I believe in - if i think it’s best
2. The clock is ticking - father time is undefeated, and sometimes you only get one go at things. I was petrified of risk taking for most of my life, but now I seek it out (in moderation) - and often times I’m glad I did. Don’t be afraid, take calculated risks, and chase your dreams - have some gumption for what you believe in and pursue it
3. Being like everyone else is not how you stand out. People will respect you more if you’re not afraid to disagree and back up what you’re saying with facts. Obviously there’s a tactful way to do this, but as someone who never wanted to have dissenting opinion - I’ve found it is appreciated more often than it is not
4. I always considered myself an introvert growing up, but if you don’t speak up working on wall street - you will be left behind. I had to find “my voice” (feels cringe writing that), but it’s true - if you don’t voice your opinion with conviction no one will respect you. This has been beneficial in other parts of my life (easier to make connections with strangers, better conversationalists, longer social battery, etc.) but I find it funny that people think I’m extroverted now, when it’s mostly a learned trait

Tell me about yourself: This is the MOST common interview question and you have to have this one down cold if you want to have a chance. I recommend taking 45-60 seconds to answer this question total. I also recommend using something I call the “funnel method” which is essentially a narrative on why your previous experiences funneled you into why you want this job today.
Here’s an Example Answer: Hi I’m Jonathan, I’m currently a junior at Duke studying economics. Coming into Duke I knew I wanted to do something mathematical and analytical in nature, but wasn’t sure how I wanted to apply it. During my sophomore summer I did research at Duke’s Fuqua school of business, and it sparked my interest in finance. This past semester I’ve joined several finance associations on campus [name them] - and got to apply my interest of math in a financial lens. I really enjoyed this, and am now [XYZ impressive title] at one of the associations. I like the broad lens through which finance lets you apply math and analysis and I would be really excited at the opportunity to apply this at [XYZ firm]

Why do you want to work at this firm and / or this industry: Again this is one that you absolutely have to have down cold. It’s an annoying question because many firms are similar to each and offer a very similar intern / analyst experience. Your answer should try to make two points - 1) demonstrating you know what the job is and you want to do it, and 2) You’re at least aware of something that firm has done, and it’s not 1 of 100 you are applying to.
Here’s an Example Answer: I interned in the finance department of [XYZ firm] last summer and really enjoyed getting to apply finance outside of the classroom setting. This helped solidify my interest in finance as a profession - but I wanted something slightly more broad - either looking at the industry holistically or working across industry verticals. I’m particularly interested in your firm / [name] because of [XYZ news article - related to something that firm worked on] and found it incredibly interesting. I’d really like to be part of a firm working on something similar to what you all have worked on in the past

This is a common interview question testing your understanding of how to calculate Enterprise Value also known as “EV”. The most simplified version of the Enterprise Value formula is:

Enterprise Value = Equity Value + Net Debt

Net Debt = Debt - Cash

So in this instance, Net Debt = $50 - $30 or $20

Enterprise Value = $100 + $20 or $120

This is not financial advice and is simplified for educational purposes.

My Top 3 Underrated Excel Functions

As someone with over 10,000 hours in Excel, I know a lot of really useful functions that help save time and improve accuracy. If you find these sorts of things helpful - you should consider following me!

—————————-

UNIQUE: The unique function is great if you have a bunch of data, especially one with duplicate values. If you =UNIQUE(Column With Values) it will return all the unique values in that column. If you copy and paste them as values - you can create a unique list

RRI: Probably one of the most slept on functions in all of Excel. This helps you calculate a CAGR / Annual Growth Rate over a number of periods - super helpful for dealing with percentages

IFERROR: This one is GOATED - a lot of times if you’re dealing with a lot of data, it’s difficult to make a formula / function that accounts for all possibilities. IFERROR is a great catch-all that allows you to account for all the scenarios where your formula / function breaks

How I Stood Out on Wall Street

Here’s what I did to stand out while I worked on Wall Street making multiple six figure bonuses over the years. You may think that you need to be a genius or have some sort advanced degree - but most of the time work ethic is what really sets most people apart.

1. Not Making The Same Mistake Twice: Wall Street is a harsh and unforgiving place, but if you’re new - people will generally understand if you don’t know a concept or make a mistake. The important thing is once it is explained to you, that you don’t make that same mistake again
2. Doing The Simple Things Well: Contrary to popular belief - most Wall Street jobs don’t require an advanced degree or much more than a high school level understanding of math. This may make it sound easy to do the simple things well - but when you’re doing five things at once, got little to no sleep the night before, and need to get something done on a super compressed timeline… doing the simple things well is not always easy
3. First One In / Last One Out: This is certainly a relic of old school Wall Street face time culture - but the importance still exists today. If you show that you are dedicated and willing to do what it takes to get the job done - senior folks will notice (this one is toxic)
4. Dressing Formally: Over the years dress codes have gotten more relaxed, but most high finance jobs will still expect you to wear business attire - this is especially true if you are an intern. You can never go wrong dressing a bit more formal than others, but if you are junior and the least formal - you will stand out for all the wrong reasons
5. Being Responsive: A big reason people get paid a lot, especially at the junior level, on Wall Street is the job can be 24/7/365 - so people will expect you to be responsive at all times (another toxic expectation)… again a relic of old school Wall Street - but something a lot of people still expect today

Where I Went To Teach Myself About Finance

1. Investopedia: As the name implies, this is like wikipedia but with a finance focus. It’s great for understanding general concepts, so if you’re ever stuck on a concept that you’re studying either for interviews, coursework, etc. this is a great resource to learn concepts in an easy to understand way. It’s not going to have crazy depth, but this should help you simplify things if you’re stuck.
2. Mergers & Inquisitions: Great resource to prepare in a weekend for a finance interview. Good combination of behavioral and technical questions to study. More of a memorization exercise than actually helping learn concepts.  3. Peak Frameworks: This is mostly focused around technicals and modeling - the guy who teaches a lot of it is an absolute unit. It will be hugely beneficial to understand technically what’s going on once you’re on the job or if you are doing case studies as part of PE recruiting
4. WSO: Wall Street Oasis (“WSO”) is an online forum for discussing finance (private equity, etc). It’s a nice resource to learn about qualitative things within the industry (culture, work/life balance, etc) but take everything you read with a grain of salt. It’s anonymous and the internet so it can be hit or miss with some really helpful and insightful information, but can also be useless garbage (so be careful!)

I’ve worked 120 Hour Weeks: Here’s What I Would Do to Survive

1. Sleeping in the bathroom: I would crumple up my suit jacket and lay it on the hand rail in the bathroom to use it as a pillow and take a nap
2. Bag musical chairs: I would constantly leave multiple bags and personal items on my desk - that way if I needed to run an errand or went home for the day at 10pm instead of 2am people wouldn’t be sure if i left yet
3. Lived two blocks from the office: I realized if I lived two blocks from the office I could save ~45 minutes on my commute every day which turned 3 hours of sleep into almost 4!!! I could also go home during the day if i ever really needed to decompress
4. I would sleep with unfolded laundry in my bed: no more efficient way to get ready in the morning than to wake up with your clothes already pulled out
5. I would sleep in my dress clothes: actually there is a more efficient way, sometimes i would sleep in my dress cloths and just roll back into the office straight away - saving another 10 or so minutes of sleep
6. Bed Office: I would usually cozy up at night with my laptop and finish some last minute work, many times I would wake up with it still on my stomach and log back on to finish up some things before heading into the office
7. Calling family and friends: i would call people at all hours of the day to cry / vent - 3am, west coast crew was getting a call… 6am my dad’s about to get up and i can talk to him!

High Paying Underrated Jobs: S&T

1. Bonuses on Wall Street can be six figures, seven figures, even eight figures and can constitute more than half of some employees’ total compensation for the year; bonuses are the carrot at the end of the stick for many people
2. All emails or any form of communication should always be written in order of seniority - addressed to the most senior person then the second most senior, third most senior, and so on - it’s one of the many ways that the hierarchy within Wall Street shows itself
3. Many firms on Wall Street, including Investment Banking & Private Equity, follow an “up-or-out” approach - meaning you either get promoted or you get let go. While it takes some people longer to get promoted than others - if you’re not doing a good job, you often won’t have a job for long
4. Many high finance firms have “target” and “non-target” schools, essentially schools they prefer to hire from and schools they don’t spend as much time (if any) recruiting from
5. Many Investment Banking analysts will leave after 2-3 years, very few analysts stay long term. They can go to private equity, other buy side firms, corporate rolls… and plenty get let go or quit without anything lined up

Step 1: Networking E-Mail
Hi [Person Name] -
Nice to connect over e-mail, it was great speaking last week at the on-campus networking event about [insert conversation topic].
I was excited to learn more about [XYZ thing you talked about] and noticed [person’s company] worked on [transaction / publicly available thing you found interesting].
If you have a few minutes sometime this week, it would be great to learn more. Happy to connect whenever is most convenient for you. I’ve also attached my resume for your reference.
Best [Because You Are the Best], Jonathan

Step 2: Networking Call
*  Beforehand: Come prepared with at least 6-7 questions
*  Questions to avoid: 1) What are the hours like?, 2) What is a typical day like?, 3) What is the group culture like?
*  Questions to ask: 1) Ask about the the article you read related to their company, 2) Ask questions where you demonstrate your ability to think (i.e. Person mentioned something, and was wondering relative to what is taught in the classroom why they didn’t do this other thing and explain why), 3) Ask about the broader industry - how do you see XYZ thing impacting you, etc.?
*  Objectives: Have a good ~30 minute conversation where you let them do as much of the talking as possible, the less you talk the better
*  After Call: Send a follow-up thank you note (see following slide) where you thank them for their time and ask them to put you in touch with others

Step 3: Thank You E-Mail
Hi [Person Namel -
Thank you again for taking the time this afternoon to connect, 1 really enjoyed learning about thing you spoke to them about where they were most engaged.
It would be great to learn more about [XYZ Company / Group] if there are other folks within the team you think would be good to speak with.
Looking forward to staying in touch.
Best Because You Are the Best],
Jonathan

First thing to realize is the people you work for are from a different generation than you - they were raised at a different point in time in the world, taught (likely similar, but) different values, and prioritize different things. IF YOU CANNOT TRY TO PUT YOURSELF IN THEIR SHOES AND TRY TO UNDERSTAND WHY THEY WANT YOU TO DO SOMETHING - YOU WILL STRUGGLE, NOT EVERYONE THINKS LIKE YOU
2. Take a ridiculous amount of notes and write them down ON A PEN AND PAPER (ancient I know), I promise you the seemingly simple thing someone walked you through at 2pm on Tuesday is going to be really hard to remember on Thursday at 3am when you didn’t sleep the night before… good thing you wrote everything down
3. Check your work once, check your work twice, check it seventeen times - CHECK YOUR WORK
4. Do not make the same mistake twice. You will make mistakes, and most reasonable people will not hold it against you - but if you start consistently making the same mistake over and over again, say goodbye to top bucket
5. Never ever be late, be PUNCTUAL - if you are the most junior person in a meeting, you should be the first one there
6. Carry printed copies into every meeting you go into - remember point one? Not everyone likes reading decks on a computer, many senior and mid-level people prefer to read something on paper
7. Look things up, but don’t rely on one-off answers instead of learning a concept - if you don’t already, better start adopting the teach a man to fish mindset… 
8. Be CONFIDENT and do NOT STRESS - easier said than done believe me, but just know that not everyone in a pinstripe suit with a Rolex is actually good at their job - some people like to talk the talk - focus on walking the walk

Five Unspoken Rules of High Finance

1. I saw in the [WSJ/FT/NYT] that your bank / group worked on [XYZ Company’s Transaction], I was curious if you or others on the team had worked on that deal any thoughts you were able to share on it?
2. One of the reasons I chose to be an econ major is that I am very interested in macroeconomic events & policy - how do you think the recent [Fed Monetary Policy / Fiscal Policy / Other Macro Event or Data] is going to impact [Bank / Group]?
 * Bonus points: share a brief informed opinion you have first, but be careful that you don’t say something obviously wrong / or sound like a know it all
3. How has your [Specific Group / Industry] evolved from [XYZ topic you personally are knowledgeable about]. 
 * Again you can share your opinion here, but idea is for this to be open ended and start a dialogue vs. you rattling off question after question to the interviewer

1. Facial hair is typical frowned upon for analysts and associates, multiple times throughout my career i got called out for having “scruff” or not being clean shaven
2. Analysts and Associates should not be wearing Rolex, Patek, AP, etc. - it looks like you have something to prove wearing a car on your wrist or worse, you’re one upping the seniors
3. Navy and grey suits are the only acceptable color. Patterns are ok, but nothing too flashy - avoid beige, charcoal, or anything with an overly elaborate pattern
4. The office clears out in order of seniority, MD’s followed by Director’s then VP’s - and eventually Associates and Analysts
5. MBA Associates are viewed as less competent to their Analyst -> Associate direct promotes until they prove themselves capable
